blurb: A broad industrial daytime plateau peaking late morning. In winter a second peak arrives at 18h as lighting lands on top of industry; in summer the afternoon sags as rooftop solar bites into net demand.

A sharp morning peak at 8h that then holds almost flat through the working day, whatever the season. An Alpine hydro system with heavy industry, electric rail and little air conditioning; the night sits at two-thirds of peak.

One of Europe's smallest grids, shaped almost entirely by the working day: a plateau from 8h to 17h peaking just before lunch, then a steep fall as cross-border commuters head home to France, Belgium and Germany.

Two seasons, two different countries. Winter peaks at 8h as electric heating and hot water switch on across the east; summer peaks at 17h as air conditioning peaks with the heat. The Lower 48 shown in Eastern time, so the west's evening smears the curve to the right.

Great Britain's grid: a winter teatime peak at 17h as lights, ovens and kettles come on while offices are still running, with the night falling below 60% of peak. In summer the peak slides to 19h and the whole curve flattens.
Two household peaks, breakfast around 8h and dinner around 18h, with a sag between them. Little heavy industry, lots of electric heating and hot water, so winter evenings are the year's peak.
Semiconductor fabs run around the clock, so the night never drops below 70% of peak. In summer air conditioning pushes the peak to 14h; in winter it shifts to an evening peak at 18h.

Reconstructed demand without outages: a high base through the day, a lull in the small hours, and the peak after sunset around 19–20h when lighting and fans switch on across the country. Power actually delivered is often less than half of this.
